metaDescription: Six pole saws at or under $200, from a CRAFTSMAN V20 kit and RYOBI 40V bare tool to a 48cc gas saw and 2-in-1 cordless kits, compared on power and reach.
expertTake: The CRAFTSMAN V20 kit is the best overall pick, because an 8-inch bar, 14 feet of reach, a 4.0Ah battery and a charger arrive in one box from a brand with parts support. The DOWILIN gas saw is the only choice here for thick, overgrown limbs. Anyone pruning only small branches should not pay for gas.
introParagraphs: This is the price band where you can choose a different class of tool, not just a different brand. Besides cordless kits, a gas two-stroke pole saw appears, trading noise and upkeep for stamina.
The sensible comparison is what the tool needs from you after purchase: a battery, mixed fuel or just an outlet. Prices move, and the $200 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: CRAFTSMAN V20 Cordless Pole Saw 14 ft with 4.0Ah Battery
products.description:
This CRAFTSMAN arrives as a complete kit with a 4.0Ah battery and charger, an 8-inch bar and a pole that reaches up to 14 feet. The maker claims up to 325 cuts per charge, a statement of real work that is more useful than a motor label. The V20 platform is widely sold, so a spare pack is easy to find.

The angled head and blade help with cutting precision, and the 4.0Ah pack is larger than the 2.0Ah cell in cheaper branded kits. Compared with the import 2-in-1 kits, it lacks a handheld mode but offers a brand with a warranty.

Keep the chain oiled and the battery indoors. It is the sensible choice for a homeowner with moderate trees. Use the three-cut method on any limb thick enough to tear bark, and never stand under the branch you are cutting. Charge the pack the night before and check the pole lock before lifting it overhead.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with moderate trees who want one box.
pros: Battery and charger included in the kit
Cut count stated by the maker

products.name: DOWILIN 48cc Gas Pole Saw 11.5-Inch Bar
products.description:
A 48cc two-stroke engine and an 11.5-inch bar make this the most capable saw in the group for thick, overgrown limbs. Gas power does not fade as a battery drains, and the engine delivers torque that cordless tools in this range cannot match. The pole has an extra 2.7 foot section for added reach.

The tradeoff is ownership. You need mixed fuel, a pull start, a spark plug and an air filter that must be kept clean, and a gas pole saw is heavier and louder than any cordless saw here. Fuel left in the carburetor over winter causes starting trouble.

Follow the maker's mix ratio exactly, drain or stabilize fuel for storage and wear hearing protection. It is the tool for someone with large trees who accepts the upkeep. Check the oil mix on the label before each fill, since too little oil scores the cylinder and too much fouls the plug. A clean air filter is the cheapest way to keep a two-stroke starting reliably.
products.bestFor: Large trees with thick limbs and a willingness to maintain an engine.
pros: Eleven and a half inch bar cuts thick limbs
No battery fade during long jobs
cons: Needs mixed fuel and engine upkeep

products.name: RYOBI 40V 10-Inch Cordless Pole Saw RY40506BTL Tool Only
products.description:
The RYOBI is a 10-inch pole saw on the brand's 40V platform, sold without a battery or charger. A 10-inch bar handles thicker limbs than the 8-inch saws, and 40V holds chain speed better than 20V when the bar is buried in wood.

The cost of the bare tool is only part of the purchase. A 40V battery and charger can cost as much as the saw, so price the full set unless you already own RYOBI 40V gear.

Store the battery indoors and keep the chain oiled. It is the right choice for RYOBI 40V owners. Compare the full cost of saw, battery and charger with the CRAFTSMAN kit before deciding. If you already own RYOBI 40V tools, the bare tool is a bargain, and a spare pack from your mower will run it.
products.bestFor: RYOBI 40V owners wanting a longer bar.

products.name: Supstable 6-Inch Cordless Pole Saw and Mini Chainsaw 16 ft 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
The Supstable uses a 6-inch bar on a pole with a claimed 16 feet of reach and ships with two 4000mAh batteries. A 6-inch bar is light at the end of a pole, which makes it comfortable for thin growth and fruit trees.

It is limited to small limbs, but the tool-free assembly and the handheld mode add convenience.

Store the packs indoors and keep the chain oiled. Because the head is light, you can cut for longer without resting, and the tool-free assembly means it goes together without a wrench. Store the batteries indoors and keep the chain clean.

products.name: Autubin Brushless 2-in-1 Cordless Pole Saw 8-Inch 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
The Autubin pairs a brushless motor with two 21V 4.0Ah packs and an 8-inch bar. The maker claims up to 120 minutes of trimming by alternating packs, which should be treated as a best case.

It converts between a 9-foot pole saw and an 8-inch mini chainsaw, giving it flexibility the CRAFTSMAN lacks.

Keep the chain oiled and the joint clean. The joint between pole and head is the part to watch, so tighten it fully and check it before each use. Treat the claimed runtime as a best case and carry the second battery.
products.bestFor: Cordless pruning with a spare pack.
cons: Wattage and runtime are marketing claims

products.name: DOOYUTOOL 2-in-1 Cordless 10-Inch Pole Saw for DeWalt 20V
products.description:
The DOOYUTOOL offers a 10-inch bar and a 4.0Ah battery, and also runs on DeWalt 20V packs. A longer bar handles thicker limbs than the 8-inch saws.

Third-party compatibility has no support from DeWalt, and the head is heavy at the end of a pole.

Keep the chain oiled. As with all third-party DeWalt-compatible tools, test the fit of your pack before the first cut and keep the packaging until you are sure it works. The longer bar helps on limbs that are already thick, but you will feel the extra head weight after a few cuts, so rest the pole on a branch fork or your strap when you can. The included 4.0Ah pack is a real plus compared with bare-tool rivals.
products.bestFor: Thicker limbs with a cordless saw.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The DOWILIN 48cc gas saw has an 11.5-inch bar and does not fade, but needs mixed fuel and engine upkeep. Cordless saws are quieter and simpler but limited by battery and voltage. Choose gas only for thick limbs. Weigh the saw at both ends of the pole in your mind, because the head weight is what you feel overhead. Check the quality of the chain brand, because a good chain stays sharp longer and cuts straighter.

The RYOBI 40V is tool only, while the CRAFTSMAN includes a 4.0Ah pack and charger. A 40V battery costs as much as the saw. Always compare full setups. Think about noise and neighbors; a gas saw is much louder than a cordless one. Plan where the limb will land before the first cut, and keep pets and children out of the area.

An 11.5-inch bar on the gas saw and 10 inch on the RYOBI and DOOYUTOOL cut thicker limbs than 6 and 8 inch bars. Rough capacity is half the bar length. Look at the oiler: gas saws and electric saws both need bar oil, and a window makes checking easy.

A 40V saw such as the RYOBI holds chain speed better than 20V and 21V saws in thick wood. The imports compensate with big packs. Check that the pole sections lock firmly, because a slipping pole can drop a running saw.

A gas engine or 10-inch bar adds weight overhead. A 6-inch head is lightest. Fatigue ends a job before the battery does. Choose a saw whose chain can be bought locally, since chains wear faster than motors.

Wear a hard hat, eye protection and hearing protection, stand outside the drop zone, and never use a metal pole near power lines. If you have only a few small limbs, a manual pole saw is cheaper, but it takes more effort. Finally, store the saw hung up or lying flat with the bar cover on, which protects the chain and the people who reach into the garage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared gas and cordless designs on torque and upkeep. The DOWILIN led on power, and the CRAFTSMAN on convenience. Torque and stamina decided the order for thick limbs, while convenience decided it for light pruning.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked batteries and chargers. The CRAFTSMAN, Autubin and Supstable include them. Kit contents were compared by battery capacity and charger inclusion.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bar and reach
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared bar length to likely limbs and discounted reach claims. Maintenance needs, such as fuel mixing or battery storage, counted as part of ownership.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed fuel, battery and parts needs over several seasons. Reach and wattage claims were discounted when they could not be checked.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We kept guidance conservative. Owner feedback patterns informed the durability view. We kept safety guidance conservative, since a pole saw drops limbs from above. Honest labeling and clear box contents scored higher than the loudest claims.

cards.text: The DOWILIN delivers steady torque on thick limbs but needs fuel mixing, an engine tune and hearing protection.

cards.label: Cordless

howToChoose.note: Pick gas for thick overgrown trees; pick cordless for ordinary pruning.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A longer bar, torque and a sharp chain. A limb should be thinner than half the bar length.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DOWILIN gas saw and RYOBI 40V are the best fits.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a brushless high-voltage saw with a long warranty. Those sit above this cap.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You prune small limbs. A cordless kit covers it.

maintenance.why: A dry chain overheats and dulls. Check the spark plug and air filter at the start of each season on the gas saw, and clean sap off the bar.

maintenance.task: Mix fuel correctly or stabilize it
maintenance.why: Wrong ratio or stale fuel causes hard starts on gas saws. Keep the pole sections clean and dry so the locks grip.
A slipping lock is a hazard overhead.
Cold or heat accelerates fade. Replace the chain when the cutters are worn down to the markings, rather than sharpening it again.

faq.q: Is a gas pole saw worth it?
faq.a: Only for thick, overgrown limbs. For ordinary pruning, cordless is simpler and quieter. Rain is a hazard for electric saws. Keep a clear drop zone every time, even for small branches.

faq.q: Do I need to buy a battery for the RYOBI?
faq.a: Yes unless you own RYOBI 40V packs. The listing is tool only. Check the bar and chain size before ordering spares.

faq.q: How thick a limb can these cut?
faq.a: Roughly half the bar length for a clean cut. Thicker limbs need a chainsaw or an arborist. Gas saws need fuel mixing, so read the manual first.

faq.q: Can I use these in the rain?
faq.a: Electric saws should stay dry. Gas saws handle damp work better. Use the three-cut method for heavy limbs.

faq.q: What safety gear do I need?
faq.a: A hard hat, eye and ear protection, and a clear drop zone. Never use a metal pole near power lines. Keep a spare chain. Gloves and sturdy boots are also worth wearing.
